title: li-fraumeni syndrome
display_name: Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
abstract: li-fraumeni syndrome (lfs) is a classic cancer predisposition disorder that is commonly associated with germline mutations of the p53 tumor suppressor gene. examination of the wide spectrum of adult-onset and childhood cancers and the distribution of p53 mutations has led to a greater understanding of cancer genotype-phenotype correlations. however, the complex lfs phenotype is not readily explained by the simple identification of germline p53 mutations in affected individuals. recent work has identified genetic events that modify the lfs phenotype. these include intragenic polymorphisms, mutations/polymorphisms of genes in the p53 regulatory pathway, as well as more global events such as aberrant copy number variation and telomere attrition. these genetic events may, in part, explain the breadth of tumor histiotypes within and across lfs families, the apparent accelerated age of onset within families, and the range of clinical outcomes among affected family members. this review will examine the clinical and genetic definitions of lfs and offer insight into how lessons learned from the study of this rare disorder may inform similar questions in other familial cancer syndromes.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: fetal alcohol syndrome
display_name: Fetal Alcohol Syndrome
abstract: objectives after completing this article, readers should be able to:alcohol is the most common human teratogen, but its significant physical and neurobehavioral effects are completely preventable. fetal alcohol syndrome (fas) was described initially in case reports by lemoine in 1968 and jones and smith in 1973. it is a pattern of physical, behavioral, and cognitive abnormalities seen in individuals exposed to alcohol in utero. the association between these findings and maternal use of alcohol during pregnancy has been well documented, with studies in both animals and humans suggesting teratogenicity from as little as one binge drinking episode in early pregnancy. the diagnostic criteria are not a result of fetal physical dependence or addiction or the presence of alcohol in the neonate at delivery; rather, they are teratogenic effects caused by in utero exposure to alcohol in the mother's blood. in 1996, following a congressional mandate that the institute of medicine and national academy of sciences study fas and related birth defects, these institutions published a review of the current understanding of fas and revised the diagnostic criteria. despite increased awareness of this preventable birth defect,new cases continue to occur in significant numbers and are routinely under-recognized by medical personnel. it is imperative that maternal alcohol use and its sequelae be considered and addressed in daily pediatric practice. the purpose of this article is to review the diagnosis, epidemiology, management, prognosis, and prevention of fas.fas represents a specific pattern of findings associated with in utero exposure to alcohol(table 1). these include: pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, minor facial anomalies(short palpebral fissures, ptosis, flat midface with upturned nose, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), and central nervous system (cns) neurodevelopmental findings(microcephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, tremors, hyperactivity, learning disabilities, cognitive impairments). infants exposed to alcohol in utero also can have major malformations, including cardiac defects, cleft lip, cleft palate, and limb reduction deformities.using the criteria established by the institute of medicine, the diagnosis of fas requires a history of maternal alcohol use during the pregnancy (proven or presumed) and elements of the three primary diagnostic categories (table 2). if maternal alcohol use is not confirmed, the diagnosis of fas may still be used, but the missing history of in utero alcohol exposure should be noted. fetal alcohol effects are minor findings that are not necessarily unique to alcohol,but that are proven to occur in association with in utero alcohol exposure. however, this term is imprecise. the institute of medicine uses the terms partial fas with confirmed maternal alcohol exposure, alcohol-related birth defects (arbd), and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (arnd) to describe alcohol-related effects not meeting the criteria for fas.the incidence of fas, arbd, and arnd has been difficult to characterize because of significant variations in study populations and methods of data collection. prospective studies and newborn discharge diagnosis data give lower incidence rates; retrospective studies and clinic-based studies tend to report higher incidence rates. the reported ranges of fas, arbd, and arnd are generally between 0.5 and 5 per 1,000 children, making alcohol exposure the most common cause of birth defects.significant controversy surrounds the amount of alcohol ingestion that presents a risk to the fetus and whether a single exposure is of greater consequence than a pattern of exposure during fetal development. initial studies of human alcohol teratogenicity examined the average amount of alcohol consumed per day during pregnancy. these studies did not demonstrate a difference between infants exposed to higher levels of alcohol or to binge drinking. however, the definitions of binge drinking were vague,and neurobehavioral and longitudinal effects were not addressed. this approach also failed to distinguish between infrequent binge drinkers who may have occasional high blood alcohol levels and mild-to-moderate regular drinkers who have lower peak blood alcohol levels but a more continuous fetal exposure.subsequent animal studies have helped define the specific gestational timing and doses of alcohol needed to produce both structural and behavioral teratogenic effects. specifically, animal studies suggest that: 1)third trimester alcohol exposure decreases brain weight and numbers of neurons, 2) peak blood alcohol concentration (affected by both dose and rate of consumption) is more critical than the same total dose with lower peak blood alcohol concentration, and 3)exposure early in the pregnancy can produce more severe and more consistent effects. an absolute threshold and critical time period for exposure is suspected, but has yet to be demonstrated.if this information is extrapolated to human alcohol teratogenicity, one can predict potential fetal effects from a single binge episode (five or more drinks in one sitting) during early development. however, the effects of low total alcohol consumption in a pattern that avoids high peak blood alcohol concentrations (ie, one to two drinks per week with no binge episodes) are unknown at this time. the prevalence of maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy increased from 12.4% to 16.3% between 1991 and 1995. frequent drinking during pregnancy, defined as more than seven drinks per week, increased from 0.8% to 3.5%. in the face of increasing maternal alcohol consumption,researchers still cannot define the threshold for alcohol toxicity in the fetus.developing organisms are uniquely susceptible to external teratogenic influences. the clinical findings in fas result from exposure of the developing fetus to toxic levels of alcohol and its metabolites at critical periods in development. the specific pathophysiology remains unknown, but may involve free radical formation that causes cellular damage in the developing tissues of the fetus. exposure in the first trimester affects organogenesis and craniofacial development, leading to minor and major malformations, such as the characteristic facial features and arbd (table 1). excessive cell death in the midline of the developing embryo may account for the development of these facial features. continuing alcohol use by the mother in later pregnancy causes decreased fetal growth that results in low birthweight and affects postnatal growth. alcohol use most likely affects cns development throughout the pregnancy, as the brain is forming early in the first trimester and is undergoing a growth spurt with maturation of the neurons in the second and third trimesters. thus,alcohol exposure at varying times in pregnancy can cause similar cns neurodevelopmental effects.alcohol use also affects fetal nutrition. obviously,alcoholism may affect maternal dietary habits and health maintenance behaviors. in addition, alcohol affects the maternal metabolism of essential nutrients by decreasing intestinal absorption, increasing renal and hepatic metabolism, and decreasing placental uptake and availability to the fetus.finally, the use of other drugs (marijuana, nicotine,caffeine) that commonly accompanies alcohol consumption can have detrimental effects on the fetus. clear delineation of alcohol-related effects is difficult in many situations where polysubstance use is present.differences in the severity and spectrum of fas have been observed based on genetic background, but it is unclear whether confounding variables may have affected the data. for example, population-based studies document up to 10-fold higher prevalence rates of fas among native american tribes than in the overall american population. however, individual tribes have markedly differing prevalence rates of fas. this may be due to confounding factors in the population-based approach, such as counting each sibling of an affected family as a separate case. if a family that included six affected children was counted as six individual cases, the local prevalence of fas would be higher than if the same family was counted as a single case (one mother delivering multiple children who had fas). the two methods of interpreting the data would result in different conclusions about the prevalence of fas within a small, closely related community, resulting in different genetic implications. one of the issues under investigation is the possible genetic susceptibility within the native american population to the teratogenic affects of alcohol. further work is necessary to establish the cause of the varying prevalence rates.the concordance of fas is higher in monozygotic twins than in dizygotic twins, supporting the concept of genetic factors in the fetal effects of alcohol. mouse embryo studies show variation in cns injury when the same dose of alcohol is given to different strains of mice,further demonstrating the variation in phenotype based on genetic background.one possible mechanism of heritable susceptibility to fas may be genetically encoded differences in alcohol dehydrogenase, the enzyme responsible for metabolizing alcohol in the liver. in mothers of children who have fas, the enzyme may be less functional, resulting in higher peak blood alcohol concentrations after the ingestion of alcohol. alternatively, the fetus may be deficient in alcohol dehydrogenase activity and, thus,less able to tolerate elevated maternal alcohol levels. clearly, the effect of genetic variation on susceptibility to in utero alcohol toxicity is an area for future research.alcohol exposure can continue postnatally if the infant is breastfeeding. alcohol is excreted in human milk at concentrations similar to blood levels, but acetaldehyde,an alcohol metabolite that may act as a teratogen, is not excreted into human milk. although the resulting serum alcohol level in the infant may be low, the combined effect of alcohol on the physiologic and social aspects of the breastfeeding relationship are significant. three points are of particular concern. first, infants'nursing behavior and total consumption of milk are adversely affected by maternal alcohol use immediately prior to a feeding. second, suckling-induced prolactin and oxytocin release are inhibited by alcohol. third,infants born to alcohol-abusing mothers have poor suck patterns and do not feed well at the breast. these findings are of significance to the nutritional and emotional aspects of the mother-infant relationship.fas is a clinical diagnosis assigned in the setting of maternal alcohol use. the typical pattern of associated features should trigger an investigation into possible fetal alcohol exposure and evaluation for other aspects of the syndrome. in many situations, the diagnosis will not be clear, requiring further evaluation by clinical geneticists and neurodevelopmental specialists, with chromosomal analysis for other causes of facial dysmorphology and neurodevelopmental abnormalities.neonatal diagnosis usually depends on characteristic facial features, suspected in utero alcohol exposure, low birthweight, poor growth, and microcephaly (tables 1 and 3). the combination of congenital malformations and poor growth should prompt an investigation into prenatal alcohol exposure. the neonate who has fas may manifest cns signs, such as irritability and hypersensitivity,hypotonia, poor feeding, and difficulty bonding with caregivers. congenital malformations and cns signs are nonspecific, however; facial features are the most useful criteria in the newborn and infant.the diagnosis of fas is easier between ages 2 and 11 years, when the facial features are still prominent and typical cns dysfunction emerges clinically. as the child approaches school age, the behavioral and cognitive aspects of the syndrome may become more pronounced, often causing difficulty with developmental tasks. from school entry through adolescence, these aspects can affect school performance and social interactions with peers. cognitive manifestations, such as memory deficits and slow information processing, are reflected in intelligence quotient (iq) testing. typical fas neurobehavioral and adaptive manifestations in the school-age child include attention deficit disorder (which may be unresponsive to stimulant medication),impulsiveness, extreme mood changes, anxiety, aggressive behavior, resistance to change, frequent temper tantrums,and difficulties with social peer interactions. in addition, these children may have speech impairment as a result of anatomic differences of the jaw, fine motor dysfunction of the oropharyngeal muscles, or hearing deficits. cognitive and behavioral difficulties also affect communication skills. a recent study estimated that the social abilities of a child who has fas plateau at the 6-year-old level and may not progress beyond this point (see thomas et al in suggested reading). the authors also showed that the interpersonal relationship skills of children who had fas were below the level of verbal iq-matched controls. it is easy to see how these issues will affect social interactions and classroom skills negatively. diagnosis in the school-age child can be made clinically if the facial features are classic, cns abnormalities are present, and maternal alcohol use during pregnancy is established. chromosomal analysis,genetic evaluation, and neurodevelopmental evaluation are important in confirming the diagnosis. as a child ages, the facial features (especially the smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and flat midface) may become harder to distinguish, making clinical diagnosis more difficult (figs. 1 and 2). "catch-up" growth may occur in adolescence, particularly in females. the cns manifestations of the syndrome and the resulting impact on cognitive skills become more prominent in adolescence. problem-solving abilities, abstract reasoning, and time and money management skills are deficient. these teenagers can be impulsive, use poor judgment, and fail to understand the consequences of their actions. in adulthood, these individuals can be isolated and withdrawn, with poor adaptive living skills. some are unable to work or manage money and often require structured living arrangements. cognitive abilities vary considerably within the group of children affected with fas. some can function successfully in a regular classroom and attain meaningful employment and even college. more severely affected children may have significant developmental delay and learning disabilities that require special programming at school and lifelong supportive services. iq scores of children who have fas range from 16 to 105, with an average of 66. in comparison, iq scores of male patients who have fragile x syndrome range from 30 to 55, and those of children who have down syndrome range from 25 to 50, with only a few testing in the 60s. fas is among the most common causes of mental retardation, but as demonstrated by the average score, most children have only mild retardation (iq scores below 70 are consistent with mental retardation). even children who have fas and normal iq scores may have significant neurobehavioral deficits and adaptive problems that affect their independence, and they are at higher risk for severe behavioral problems and psychiatric disorders. approximately 62% of patients who have fas have severe behavioral problems compared with 15% to 32% of those who have down syndrome. individuals who have fas may face more difficulties holding a job, maintaining social relationships, and living independently than people who have down syndrome and similar or even lower iqs.for example, consider john, a 7-year-old boy who was exposed to alcohol in utero and has facial features consistent with fas, height at the 10th percentile,weight less than the 5th percentile, and head circumference less than the 5th percentile for age. fas was diagnosed clinically in his first year of life based on the in utero alcohol exposure, growth retardation,microcephaly, and facial features in conjunction with a negative evaluation for genetic and other known disorders. his home environment was evaluated, support services were arranged for his mother, and evaluation for alcohol-related disability was arranged for his older sister. john's iq is 75. speech delay affects his school performance and social interactions. he is having increasing difficulties with attention during the school day, aggressiveness toward peers, mood swings, and temper tantrums. these further impair his school performance and peer interactions. john also has specific difficulties with math and organizational skills. he will require evaluation for supportive behavioral and educational services, despite his normal iq, and for hearing impairment and will need close monitoring for other problems that may develop in the future.other social and pathologic processes affect children who are exposed to alcohol in utero. labeling affected children as having arnd may overlook additional negative influences on their cognition and behavior. for example,many children who have fas and arnd also live with poverty, unstable home situations, lack of emotional support systems, and inappropriate educational resources. these situations can cause fear, depression, and frustration that may be misinterpreted as alcohol-related behavioral problems. it can be easy to blame all of a child's difficulties on prenatal alcohol exposure,when part of the problem may be ongoing exposure to external influences.the differential diagnosis of fas is important because the fas phenotype is variable and may be difficult to distinguish from other conditions. the physical features can be confused with those of aarskog syndrome, williams syndrome, noonan syndrome, dubowitz syndrome, bloom syndrome, fetal hydantoin syndrome, and maternal phenylketonuria fetal effects (table 4). the neurobehavioral features may be similar to those seen in fragile x syndrome, the 22q11 deletion syndromes, turner syndrome, or opitz syndrome (table 5). when contemplating the diagnosis of fas, it is important to consider these and other genetic, metabolic,toxicologic, and neurodevelopmental syndromes and to seek consultation as necessary.the early diagnosis of fas benefits infants and children. medical intervention, including evaluation of growth and nutrition, management of medical issues related to birth defects, and identification of other medical issues specific to the child in question, is crucial to the care of the child who has fas. other appropriate interventions, in the form of educational evaluation and support and community resources, can be accessed and put into place early, allowing the child to reach his or her maximum potential. developmental delay,functional abilities, speech abilities, and social/behavioral interactions may improve with timely implementation of resource programs (although it is yet to be demonstrated that iq can change with appropriate supports in fas). correct diagnosis may result in recognition of the maternal problem and access to community resources for her. because many of these children live in impaired homes resulting from continued alcohol use by the parent, any additional support of the family may improve the social circumstances and,therefore, optimize the abilities of the child.in addition, other siblings may be diagnosed with fas,arbd, or arnd. the youngest child in a family may be the most severely affected (as a result of prolonged maternal addiction and worsening maternal health) and, thus, the most easily detected. diagnosis and appropriate interventions may be facilitated in mildly affected older siblings once the initial child has been diagnosed. it is, therefore, important to evaluate all siblings of a child who has fas.the national organization on fetal alcohol syndrome(nofas) is a nonprofit group that provides educational and supportive resources for families affected by fas and is involved in educating medical professionals and the public about the effects of alcohol during pregnancy. their web site (www.nofas.org) has information on numerous support groups, newsletters, and informational sources about fas that may be useful to parents,caregivers, and medical practitioners. nofas also can be reached at 216 g street northeast, washington, dc 20002.the pediatrician has a multifaceted role in the care of the child who has fas. obviously, the initial diagnosis is important, and whenever possible the child should be identified in early infancy. this requires a high index of suspicion and a pediatrician who is prepared to raise the issue with the family in a straightforward but supportive manner. the pediatrician also must consider fas during evaluation of the older child or teenager who demonstrates behavioral problems, poor school performance, and impulsivity. although the differential diagnosis for these findings is broad, it is important to elicit the family and social history that may suggest fas, arbd, or arnd. if a diagnosis is not clear, the pediatrician should make appropriate referrals for further genetic and neurodevelopmental evaluation. the pediatrician needs to be familiar with the social and educational resources in the community that can support families. pediatricians need to facilitate access to such resources, encourage development of the full potential of the affected child, and provide ongoing medical care.fas is preventable. the cost of this condition in stress to the family, medical resources, and lost human potential is tremendous. although accurate diagnosis and access to the appropriate resources is extremely important, much more can be done. in 2000, the american academy of pediatrics (aap) published updated recommendations for advocacy within the community and health-care setting regarding alcohol use in pregnancy(table 6). the aap supports abstinence by pregnant women because there is no established safe level of alcohol consumption during pregnancy. in addition, the aap recommends counseling women of childbearing age about the effects of alcohol on the fetus and supports legislation to warn of the effects of prenatal alcohol in prominent places (such as in advertisements for alcohol and at marriage licensing bureaus). the pediatrician is an integral part of this community effort to prevent fas.

title: a common allele in the oxytocin receptor gene ( oxtr ) impacts prosocial temperament and human hypothalamic-limbic structure and function
display_name: A common allele in the oxytocin receptor gene ( OXTR ) impacts prosocial temperament and human hypothalamic-limbic structure and function
abstract: the evolutionarily highly conserved neuropeptide oxytocin is a key mediator of social and emotional behavior in mammals, including humans. a common variant (rs53576) in the oxytocin receptor gene ( oxtr ) has been implicated in social-behavioral phenotypes, such as maternal sensitivity and empathy, and with neuropsychiatric disorders associated with social impairment, but the intermediate neural mechanisms are unknown. here, we used multimodal neuroimaging in a large sample of healthy human subjects to identify structural and functional alterations in oxtr risk allele carriers and their link to temperament. activation and interregional coupling of the amygdala during the processing of emotionally salient social cues was significantly affected by genotype. in addition, evidence for structural alterations in key oxytocinergic regions emerged, particularly in the hypothalamus. these neural characteristics predicted lower levels of reward dependence, specifically in male risk allele carriers. our findings identify sex-dependent mechanisms impacting the structure and function of hypothalamic-limbic circuits that are of potential clinical and translational significance.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: effect of genetic variation in the organic cation transporter 1 (oct1) on metformin action
display_name: Effect of genetic variation in the organic cation transporter 1 (OCT1) on metformin action
abstract: metformin is among the most widely prescribed drugs for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. organic cation transporter 1 (oct1) plays a role in the hepatic uptake of metformin, but its role in the therapeutic effects of the drug, which involve activation of amp-activated protein kinase (ampk), is unknown. recent studies have shown that human oct1 is highly polymorphic. we investigated whether oct1 plays a role in the action of metformin and whether individuals with oct1 polymorphisms have reduced response to the drug. in mouse hepatocytes, deletion of oct1 resulted in a reduction in the effects of metformin on ampk phosphorylation and gluconeogenesis. in oct1-deficient mice the glucose-lowering effects of metformin were completely abolished. seven nonsynonymous polymorphisms of oct1 that exhibited reduced uptake of metformin were identified. notably, oct1-420del (allele frequency of about 20% in white americans), previously shown to have normal activity for model substrates, had reduced activity for metformin. in clinical studies, the effects of metformin in glucose tolerance tests were significantly lower in individuals carrying reduced function polymorphisms of oct1. collectively, the data indicate that oct1 is important for metformin therapeutic action and that genetic variation in oct1 may contribute to variation in response to the drug.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: comparison of universal genetic testing vs guideline-directed targeted testing for patients with hereditary cancer syndrome
display_name: Comparison of Universal Genetic Testing vs Guideline-Directed Targeted Testing for Patients With Hereditary Cancer Syndrome
abstract: this prospective, multicenter cohort study found that universal multigene panel testing among patients with solid tumor cancer was associated with an increased detection of heritable variants over the predicted yield of targeted testing based on guidelines. nearly 30% of patients with high-penetrance variants had modifications in their treatment. uptake of cascade fvt was low despite being offered at no cost.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: multidrug-resistant plasmodium vivax associated with severe and fatal malaria: a prospective study in papua, indonesia
display_name: Multidrug-Resistant Plasmodium vivax Associated with Severe and Fatal Malaria: A Prospective Study in Papua, Indonesia
abstract: in this region with established high-grade chloroquine resistance to both pv and pf, pv is associated with severe and fatal malaria particularly in young children. the epidemiology of p. vivax needs to be re-examined elsewhere where chloroquine resistance is increasing.

title: implications of visuospatial skills and executive functions for learning mathematics
display_name: Implications of Visuospatial Skills and Executive Functions for Learning Mathematics

authorships.name: Claire E. Cameron
institutions: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

abstract: the purpose of this article is to review the literature and apply a developmental neuroscience perspective in investigating the role of two interrelated cognitive processes executive functions (efs) and visuospatial (vs) skills which have been empirically and theoretically linked to children s mathematics achievement. to illustrate, we provide evidence of the importance of efs and vs skills for mathematics learning by examining and comparing the distinct cognitive profiles of individuals with autism spectrum disorder and williams syndrome. by simultaneously considering two cognitive processes that are implicated in mathematics, we offer insight into the underlying mechanisms by which efs and vs skills support children s learning and acquisition of mathematical skills, as well as how neuroscience research may successfully inform educational practice.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: a role for atr in the dna damage-induced phosphorylation of p53
display_name: A role for ATR in the DNA damage-induced phosphorylation of p53
abstract: phosphorylation at ser-15 may be a critical event in the up-regulation and functional activation of p53 during cellular stress. in this report we provide evidence that the atm-rad3-related protein atr regulates phosphorylation of ser-15 in dna-damaged cells. overexpression of catalytically inactive atr (atrki) in human fibroblasts inhibited ser-15 phosphorylation in response to gamma-irradiation and uv light. in gamma-irradiated cells, atrki expression selectively interfered with late-phase ser-15 phosphorylation, whereas atrki blocked uv-induced ser-15 phosphorylation in a time-independent manner. atr phosphorylated p53 at ser-15 and ser-37 in vitro, suggesting that p53 is a target for phosphorylation by atr in dna-damaged cells.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: a randomized trial of yoga for adolescents with irritable bowel syndrome
display_name: A Randomized Trial of Yoga for Adolescents with Irritable Bowel Syndrome
abstract: background: adolescents with irritable bowel syndrome (ibs) frequently experience interference with everyday activities. mind body approaches such as yoga have been recommended as interventions for patients with ibs. despite promising results among adult samples, there have been limited studies exploring the efficacy of yoga with pediatric patients. objective: to conduct a preliminary randomized study of yoga as treatment for adolescents with ibs. methods: twenty five adolescents aged 11 to 18 years with ibs were randomly assigned to either a yoga or wait list control group. before the intervention, both groups completed questionnaires assessing gastrointestinal symptoms, pain, functional disability, coping, anxiety and depression. the yoga intervention consisted of a 1 h instructional session, demonstration and practice, followed by four weeks of daily home practice guided by a video. after four weeks, adolescents repeated the baseline questionnaires. the wait list control group then received the yoga intervention and four weeks later completed an additional set of questionnaires. results: adolescents in the yoga group reported lower levels of functional disability, less use of emotion focused avoidance and lower anxiety following the intervention than adolescents in the control group. when the pre and postintervention data for the two groups were combined, adolescents had significantly lower scores for gastrointestinal symptoms and emotion focused avoidance following the yoga intervention. adolescents found the yoga to be helpful and indicated they would continue to use it to manage their ibs. conclusions: yoga holds promise as an intervention for adolescents with ibs.

title: early-life programming of later-life brain and behavior: a critical role for the immune system
display_name: Early-life programming of later-life brain and behavior: a critical role for the immune system
abstract: the immune system is well characterized for its critical role in host defense. far beyond this limited role however, there is mounting evidence for the vital role the immune system plays within the brain, in both normal, "homeostatic" processes (e.g., sleep, metabolism, memory), as well as in pathology, when the dysregulation of immune molecules may occur. this recognition is especially critical in the area of brain development. microglia and astrocytes, the primary immunocompetent cells of the cns, are involved in every major aspect of brain development and function, including synaptogenesis, apoptosis, and angiogenesis. cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (tnf)alpha, interleukin [il]-1beta, and il-6 are produced by glia within the cns, and are implicated in synaptic formation and scaling, long-term potentiation, and neurogenesis. importantly, cytokines are involved in both injury and repair, and the conditions underlying these distinct outcomes are under intense investigation and debate. evidence from both animal and human studies implicates the immune system in a number of disorders with known or suspected developmental origins, including schizophrenia, anxiety/depression, and cognitive dysfunction. we review the evidence that infection during the perinatal period of life acts as a vulnerability factor for later-life alterations in cytokine production, and marked changes in cognitive and affective behaviors throughout the remainder of the lifespan. we also discuss the hypothesis that long-term changes in brain glial cell function underlie this vulnerability.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: cellular stress responses: cell survival and cell death
display_name: Cellular Stress Responses: Cell Survival and Cell Death

authorships.name: Adrienne M. Gorman
institutions: Ollscoil na Gaillimhe – University of Galway

authorships.name: Afshin Samali
institutions: Ollscoil na Gaillimhe – University of Galway

abstract: cells can respond to stress in various ways ranging from the activation of survival pathways to the initiation of cell death that eventually eliminates damaged cells. whether cells mount a protective or destructive stress response depends to a large extent on the nature and duration of the stress as well as the cell type. also, there is often the interplay between these responses that ultimately determines the fate of the stressed cell. the mechanism by which a cell dies (i.e., apoptosis, necrosis, pyroptosis, or autophagic cell death) depends on various exogenous factors as well as the cell's ability to handle the stress to which it is exposed. the implications of cellular stress responses to human physiology and diseases are manifold and will be discussed in this review in the context of some major world health issues such as diabetes, parkinson's disease, myocardial infarction, and cancer.

title: functional significance and induction by solar radiation of ultraviolet-absorbing sunscreens in field-grown soybean crops
display_name: Functional Significance and Induction by Solar Radiation of Ultraviolet-Absorbing Sunscreens in Field-Grown Soybean Crops

abstract: abstract colorless phenylpropanoid derivatives are known to protect plants from ultraviolet (uv) radiation, but their photoregulation and physiological roles under field conditions have not been investigated in detail. here we describe a fast method to estimate the degree of uv penetration into photosynthetic tissue, which is based on chlorophyll fluorescence imaging. in arabidopsis this technique clearly separated the uv-hypersensitive transparent testa (tt) tt5 andtt6 mutants from the wild type (wt) andtt3, tt4, and tt7 mutants. in field-grown soybean (glycine max), we found significant differences in uv penetration among cultivars with different levels of leaf phenolics, and between plants grown under contrasting levels of solar uv-b. the reduction in uv penetration induced by ambient uv-b had direct implications for dna integrity in the underlying leaf tissue; thus, the number of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers caused by a short exposure to solar uv-b was much larger in leaves with high uv transmittance than in leaves pretreated with solar uv-b to increase the content phenylpropanoids. most of the phenylpropanoid response to solar uv in field-grown soybeans was induced by the uv-b component ( 315 nm). our results indicate that phenolic sunscreens in soybean are highly responsive to the wavelengths that are most affected by variations in ozone levels, and that they play an important role in uv protection in the field.

title: role of noninvasive testing in the clinical evaluation of women with suspected coronary artery disease
display_name: Role of Noninvasive Testing in the Clinical Evaluation of Women With Suspected Coronary Artery Disease
abstract: cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality for women in the united states. coronary heart disease, which includes coronary atherosclerotic disease, myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndromes, and angina, is the largest subset of this mortality, with >240 000 women dying annually from the disease. atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (cad) is the focus of this consensus statement. research continues to report underrecognition and underdiagnosis of cad as contributory to high mortality rates in women. timely and accurate diagnosis can significantly reduce cad mortality for women; indeed, once the diagnosis is made, it does appear that current treatments are equally effective at reducing risk in both women and men. as such, noninvasive diagnostic and prognostic testing offers the potential to identify women at increased cad risk as the basis for instituting preventive and therapeutic interventions. nevertheless, the recent evidence-based practice program report from the agency for healthcare research and quality noted the paucity of women enrolled in diagnostic research studies. consequently, much of the evidence supporting contemporary recommendations for noninvasive diagnostic studies in women is extrapolated from studies conducted predominantly in cohorts of middle-aged men. the majority of diagnostic and prognostic evidence in cardiac imaging in women and men has been derived from observational registries and referral populations that are affected by selection and other biases. thus, a better understanding of the potential impact of sex differences on noninvasive cardiac testing in women may greatly improve clinical decision making. this consensus statement provides a synopsis of available evidence on the role of the exercise ecg and cardiac imaging modalities, both those in common use as well as developing technologies that may add clinical value to the diagnosis and risk assessment of the symptomatic and asymptomatic woman with suspected cad.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: adherence to maintenance-phase antidepressant medication as a function of patient beliefs about medication
display_name: Adherence to Maintenance-Phase Antidepressant Medication as a Function of Patient Beliefs About Medication
abstract: patients given maintenance antidepressants vary widely in adherence. this variation is primarily explained by the balance between their perceptions of need and harmfulness of antidepressant medication, in that adherence is lowest when perceived harm exceeds perceived need, and highest when perceived need exceeds perceived harm. we speculate on ways to tailor adherence strategies to patient beliefs. subsequent research should determine whether patients' perceptions about medication predict depression outcomes, can be used to improve clinical management, and respond to behavioral intervention.
classification_path: Medical and Health Science > Basic Medicine > Medical Genetics > Clinical Genetics

title: normal weight obesity: a risk factor for cardiometabolic dysregulation and cardiovascular mortality
display_name: Normal weight obesity: a risk factor for cardiometabolic dysregulation and cardiovascular mortality
abstract: normal weight obesity, defined as the combination of normal bmi and high bf content, is associated with a high prevalence of cardiometabolic dysregulation, metabolic syndrome, and cv risk factors. in women, nwo is independently associated with increased risk for cv mortality.

title: clinical risk factors, dna variants, and the development of type 2 diabetes
display_name: Clinical Risk Factors, DNA Variants, and the Development of Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: as compared with clinical risk factors alone, common genetic variants associated with the risk of diabetes had a small effect on the ability to predict the future development of type 2 diabetes. the value of genetic factors increased with an increasing duration of follow-up.
